analysis.one_liner: Requires drug companies to disclose deals that delay generic drugs to antitrust regulators.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed the bill unanimously on November 18, 2002, but the House never voted on it and it died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: Brand-name drug makers sometimes pay generic drug makers to keep cheaper copies off the market. This bill would not ban those deals, but it would force both companies to file them with the Justice Department and the Federal Trade Commission within ten business days, so regulators could decide whether they violate antitrust laws. Companies that failed to file would face fines of up to $11,000 per day, and courts could make unfiled agreements unenforceable.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and families who pay for prescription drugs. Generic drugs typically cost far less than brand-name versions, so any deal that keeps a generic off the market keeps prices high. Giving antitrust enforcers a timely look at these deals would help the Federal Trade Commission and the Justice Department police them, as the bill's own findings acknowledge that competition among drug makers can significantly reduce what Americans spend on prescriptions.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires every agreement between a brand-name drug company and a generic applicant, before the generic reaches the market, to be filed with the Assistant Attorney General and the FTC within ten business days, covering deals about manufacturing, marketing, sale, or the 180-day exclusivity period.
Companies that fail to file face a civil penalty of up to $11,000 per day, and a federal court can order compliance or even make an unfiled agreement unenforceable for the period it was not filed.
Congress's stated purpose is that timely notice will make enforcement of existing antitrust laws more effective and that competition can significantly reduce what Americans spend on prescriptions.
The bill passed the Senate by unanimous consent on November 18, 2002, meaning no senator on either side opposed it.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name and generic drug companies, which would bear the filing obligation and potential $11,000-per-day fines. The larger cost falls on brand-name drug makers, whose private deals with generic competitors would become visible to antitrust regulators for the first time. Taxpayers would fund the added enforcement workload at the FTC and the Justice Department's Antitrust Division.

drawbacks.text: The bill only requires disclosure; it does not ban pay-for-delay deals. Companies could continue striking agreements that keep generics off the market as long as they file them, leaving the remedy to later antitrust cases.

Filed agreements are exempt from the Freedom of Information Act and cannot be made public except in a court or agency proceeding, so the public itself would never see the deals — only regulators and Congress would.
Companies face a compliance burden and fines of up to $11,000 per day for missed filings, though the law exempts ordinary supply, equipment, employment, and packaging contracts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is indirect but real: regulators get an early look at deals that can keep cheaper generics off the market, and the potential court remedy of voiding unfiled agreements gives the disclosure rule teeth. The costs are modest compliance burdens on drug companies. The bill's main weakness is that it stops at notice and does not itself prohibit the deals, so its value depends entirely on whether the FTC and the Justice Department actually challenge the agreements they see.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it by unanimous consent in mid-November 2002, but the House sent it to two committees and then to a health subcommittee, and no House vote ever came before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Patrick Leahy introduced the bill on April 6, 2001, and it was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which he chaired.

The Senate Judiciary Committee ordered the bill favorably reported on October 18, 2001, and reported it with an amendment in the nature of a substitute on June 20, 2002, placing it on the Senate calendar.
On November 18, 2002, the Senate took the bill up by unanimous consent, agreed to the committee substitute as amended, and passed it by unanimous consent — no senator opposed it.

The House received the bill on November 19, 2002 and referred it to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary Committees; on November 22 it was referred to the Health Subcommittee, where it sat with no further action.
The 107th Congress ended January 3, 2003, so the bill died in a House subcommittee without ever reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug companies benefited, because deals with generic competitors that might have drawn antitrust scrutiny remained undisclosed. The FTC and Justice Department also lost a tool they never got; no one paid a price for the bill's failure.

sides.party_line_note: The Senate passed the bill by unanimous consent with no recorded opposition, and its cosponsors included senators of both parties — five Democrats and one Republican.

industries.note: The bill would have forced them to file every pre-market deal with generic applicants with the FTC and Justice Department within ten business days, exposing agreements that keep cheaper generics off the market to antitrust review. Their interest was in keeping those deals private, which runs against patients paying brand-name prices longer.

Generic applicants faced the same filing duty and fines, but the deals being policed are ones that delay generic entry, so stronger antitrust oversight tends to open the market sooner for generics and their customers.
